questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the Von Neumann architecture?
options: Instructions and data are stored in separate memories with separate buses
Instructions and data share a single memory and are fetched over the same bus
Every instruction executes in exactly one clock cycle
Programs cannot modify their own instructions at runtime
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — the stored-program concept keeps instructions and data in one shared memory.
questions.feedbackWrong: Von Neumann's key feature is shared memory for instructions and data over a common bus.

mistakes.misconception: Confuses Von Neumann with Harvard architecture — separate memories/buses is the Harvard design.
mistakes.correction: Von Neumann uses one memory for both instructions and data; Harvard separates them.

mistakes.misconception: Confuses architecture with RISC design goals; single-cycle execution is not a Von Neumann property.
mistakes.correction: The Von Neumann fetch-decode-execute cycle typically takes multiple clock cycles per instruction.

questions.prompt: What does the Program Counter (PC) hold during the fetch-decode-execute cycle?
options: The instruction currently being executed
The address of the next instruction to be fetched
The data value most recently read from memory
The memory address of the last arithmetic result
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — the PC holds the address of the next instruction.
questions.feedbackWrong: The PC is an address register: it points at the next instruction to fetch.

mistakes.misconception: Confuses the PC with the CIR — the Current Instruction Register holds the instruction being executed.
mistakes.correction: The PC holds the address of the next instruction; the fetched instruction itself goes to the CIR.

questions.prompt: A processor upgrades its address bus from 16 bits to 32 bits. What is the direct effect?
options: Each memory location can now store twice as much data
The processor can directly address a larger memory space
Data transfers happen twice as fast
Instructions execute in half the time
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — address bus width determines the number of unique addresses: 2^32 vs 2^16 locations.
questions.feedbackWrong: Address bus width determines how many memory locations can be addressed, not speed or location size.

mistakes.misconception: Confuses the address bus with the data bus — location capacity depends on the data bus/word size.
mistakes.correction: The data bus width governs how much data moves per transfer; the address bus width governs how many locations exist.

mistakes.misconception: Assumes wider buses always mean faster transfer.
mistakes.correction: The address bus carries only addresses, not data payload — it does not affect transfer speed.

questions.prompt: Explain how cache memory improves the performance of a CPU.

markScheme.text: Cache is fast memory located on or very close to the CPU, so access is much quicker than main memory (RAM).
It stores frequently/recently used instructions and data, so the CPU often avoids slower RAM accesses (cache hit).
This reduces the effect of the Von Neumann bottleneck / reduces average memory access time, so fewer clock cycles are wasted waiting.

mistakes.misconception: Overstates cache capacity — cache is small and cannot hold all program data.
mistakes.correction: Cache holds only a working subset of recently or frequently used data; bulk storage remains in RAM.

mistakes.misconception: Locates cache inside main memory rather than as separate fast memory near the CPU.
mistakes.correction: Cache sits between the CPU and RAM (on-chip L1/L2/L3); it is distinct from and much faster than RAM.

questions.prompt: A student writes a game in a high-level language. Compare compiling and interpreting the code, giving one reason a developer might choose each approach.
questions.guidance: Structure your answer around translation timing, runtime speed, and debugging/distribution.

markScheme.text: A compiler translates the whole source program into machine code before execution, producing an executable file.
An interpreter translates and executes the source code line by line at runtime.
Reason to compile: the compiled executable runs faster at runtime / does not need the source code or a translator present, protecting intellectual property.
Reason to interpret: errors are reported as soon as the offending line runs, making debugging easier during development / no recompilation cycle needed for each change.

questions.prompt: Describe two functions performed by an assembler when translating assembly language, other than converting mnemonics to opcodes.

markScheme.text: Resolves symbolic labels/addresses — replacing label references with actual memory addresses.
Handles directives — e.g. reserving memory for data/constants or setting the origin address.
Performs macro expansion and/or reports syntax errors with line references.

questions.prompt: Describe the role of the Memory Address Register (MAR) and Memory Data Register (MDR) during the fetch stage of the fetch-decode-execute cycle.

markScheme.text: The address of the next instruction is copied from the PC into the MAR.
The MAR drives the address bus so that memory location is read.
The instruction/data read from memory is transferred along the data bus into the MDR.
The contents of the MDR are copied to the CIR for decoding (and the PC increments).

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of pipelining in a modern CPU?
options: To execute several instructions at different stages simultaneously, increasing throughput
To allow multiple programs to share the same memory space
To remove the need for cache memory
To make each individual instruction complete faster
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — pipelining overlaps fetch/decode/execute stages so throughput rises.
questions.feedbackWrong: Pipelining overlaps instruction stages across the processor, increasing throughput rather than speeding up any single instruction.

mistakes.misconception: Believes pipelining reduces latency of individual instructions.
mistakes.correction: Each instruction still passes through every stage; pipelining improves throughput (instructions per unit time), not single-instruction latency.

questions.prompt: A computer has a 24-bit address bus. How many distinct memory locations can it directly address? Give your answer as a number of locations (in millions, to 1 decimal place, in Mega-locations where 1 Mega-location = 2^20 locations).
Explain why a linker is needed when building a large program made of multiple object files and library routines.

markScheme.text: Object files reference external symbols (library routines/other modules) whose addresses are unknown at compile time.
The linker resolves these references, combining modules into a single executable with correct cross-references.
This enables modular development and reuse of pre-compiled libraries without recompiling everything.

questions.prompt: State two characteristics that typically distinguish an embedded system from a general-purpose computer.

markScheme.text: Dedicated to a single/specific function (e.g. washing machine controller) rather than running arbitrary user software.
Any one of: constrained resources (limited memory/power); software often in ROM/firmware; real-time operation; no conventional user interface.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a memory-management function of an operating system?
options: Converting virtual memory addresses to physical addresses using paging
Checking user passwords at login
Compressing files to save disk space
Rendering windows and icons on screen
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — virtual-to-physical address translation and paging are core OS memory management.
questions.feedbackWrong: Memory management includes paging, virtual memory translation, and allocation of memory to processes.

mistakes.misconception: Attributes the user interface (a separate OS function) to memory management.
mistakes.correction: Memory management concerns allocation, paging and virtual memory; rendering belongs to the UI layer.
